title: The three-mile-an-hour God
hookLine: Kosuke Koyama: God walks at human pace, the speed of love

lines: A RICE FIELD, A WATER BUFFALO.
A TEACHER WITH A BAG OF BOOKS.
cards: A rice field in the north of Thailand. A farmer is up to his shins in mud, behind a water buffalo that moves exactly as fast as a water buffalo wants to move.

At the edge of the field stands Kosuke Koyama, a Japanese missionary and teacher. He has come to teach the Bible, his bag full of theology from Europe, and he starts to wonder whether he has been in too much of a hurry.
What would the gospel sound like if it started here, in the mud, at the buffalo's pace? That question became a short book with an odd title: today's word.

teach.h: WE WALK AT ABOUT THREE MILES AN HOUR.
teach.b: The book is Three Mile an Hour God. His idea: we walk at about three miles an hour, and so, he says, does God's love. It doesn't arrive by express train.
It walks beside you. First, the wilderness.

Moses tells Israel, in the King James words: "thou shalt remember all the way which the LORD thy God led thee these forty years in the wilderness, to humble thee, and to prove thee, to know what was in thine heart."
Forty years, on foot. Why so long?
Koyama's answer: the lesson was trust, and trust can't be rushed. A people learning to depend on God one day of manna at a time. Second, Jesus, walking village to village.
On the road to Emmaus, two grieving friends are trudging home when a stranger falls in beside them.
Luke says: "Jesus himself drew near, and went with them." He doesn't fly in with the answer. He walks their road at their pace, listening first.
Third, the contrast. Koyama watched a world that prized speed: faster machines, faster results. He didn't call speed evil.
He said love has its own speed, and it's slow. You can't love someone at a hundred miles an hour; you have to stop, and look, and walk with them. Fourth, the buffalo again.

His farmers didn't need a theology flown in from elsewhere. Koyama tried to start from their life, their soil, their pace. That, he thought, is how God came to us: at walking speed, in the dust of one place.

how: Some Christians practice slow walking prayer, on pilgrimage routes, in labyrinths or simply around a neighborhood, and some churches hold walks that retell the Emmaus road.

games.q: two friends are walking home, grieving, arguing about what just happened. you could tell them everything at once. what do you do?
o: give them the answer straight away and move on.
fall in beside them and walk at their pace.
wait at their house for them to arrive.
games.why: Luke says "Jesus himself drew near, and went with them": he walks the road with them and listens first. that's Koyama's three-mile-an-hour God.

practice: Take a few steps much slower than usual, heel, sole, toes, or, if you can't walk right now, slow your breath to an unhurried stride. Let your body find the speed of someone who isn't late for anything.
If you pray, picture walking beside someone on a dusty road; if not, notice what this speed shows you that a run would miss.

wordCard.voice: The three-mile-an-hour God. Kosuke Koyama's picture of a love that walks at human pace, through the wilderness and down the Emmaus road.

carryVoice: Your line: the speed of love. Slow on purpose, and right beside you. Until tomorrow.
